title: MARPOL — Marine Pollution Convention
description: MARPOL 73/78 is the principal international convention controlling pollution from ships, covering oil, noxious liquid substances, packaged harmful goods, sewage, garbage, and air emissions. Its six Annexes establish discharge standards, record-keeping obligations, and equipment requirements applicable across the global fleet. Seafarers interacting with Oil Record Books, Garbage Record Books, or fuel changeover logs are working directly under MARPOL. Understanding which Annexes apply, what Special Areas restrict, and how Port State Control inspects is essential for every shipboard officer.

episodes.title: What is MARPOL and Why It Exists
The Six Annexes at a Glance
Flag State vs. Port State Control under MARPOL

seasons.title: Season 3 — Annex V: Garbage at Sea

episodes.title: What Can and Cannot Be Discharged
Placards and Garbage Management in Practice

title: COLREGS — Collision Regulations
description: The Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (1972) sets the rules of the road for every vessel on navigable waters worldwide. COLREGS covers look-out duties, safe speed, risk of collision assessment, give-way and stand-on obligations, traffic separation schemes, and the full system of navigation lights, shapes, and sound signals. Every officer of the watch depends on fluent knowledge of these rules — and collision investigations consistently show COLREGS violations at their root.

episodes.title: What COLREGS Are and Who They Apply To

title: MLC 2006 — Maritime Labour Convention
description: The Maritime Labour Convention 2006 is the "fourth pillar" of international maritime law, consolidating over 65 ILO instruments into a single comprehensive framework for seafarer rights and welfare. In force since 2013 and covering over 160,000 ships, MLC sets minimum standards for employment agreements, wages, hours of rest, accommodation, food, medical care, and complaint procedures. It is enforced through the Maritime Labour Certificate, the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance, and Port State Control inspections worldwide.

episodes.title: Structure: Articles, Regulations, and the Code
Title 4 — Health Protection and Medical Care
Title 4 — Social Security and Accident Compensation

title: Load Lines Convention 1966
description: The International Convention on Load Lines 1966 establishes the minimum freeboard (the distance from the waterline to the freeboard deck) that a ship must maintain for safe operation in different ocean zones and seasons. Rooted in Samuel Plimsoll's 19th-century campaign against overloaded ships, the Convention assigns each vessel a set of load line marks that are physically cut into the hull and certified by a recognized organization. Loading a ship below her permitted mark in a given zone is an offense regardless of whether it appears to improve stability.

episodes.title: What is a Load Line and Why It Exists

title: SAR Convention 1979 — Search and Rescue
description: The International Convention on Maritime Search and Rescue (1979) established a global framework dividing the world's oceans into SAR Regions, each assigned to a coastal State responsible for coordinating rescue operations. It works in tandem with GMDSS, SOLAS Chapter V, and the IAMSAR Manual to create a coherent system from distress alert to rescue completion. Every ship master has legal duties under SAR 1979 — including the obligation to assist persons in distress and to act on instructions from Maritime Rescue Coordination Centers.

episodes.title: The Master's Duty to Render Assistance

title: Tonnage Convention 1969
description: The International Convention on Tonnage Measurement of Ships 1969 standardized how the size of a vessel is measured and expressed, replacing a patchwork of national systems. Gross Tonnage and Net Tonnage are not weights but volumetric measures that drive port dues, canal fees, SOLAS applicability thresholds, and manning requirements. Understanding the difference between GT, NT, and DWT — and knowing why the same physical ship may carry different tonnage figures under different measurement rules — is relevant to officers involved in commercial operations, port entry, and regulatory compliance.

title: SUA Convention — Suppression of Unlawful Acts
description: The Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts Against the Safety of Maritime Navigation (Rome 1988, updated by the 2005 Protocol) criminalizes acts of terrorism, seizure, and violence directed at ships or using ships as weapons. Born from the 1985 Achille Lauro hijacking, SUA created the legal framework for prosecuting maritime terrorism regardless of where it occurs or the nationalities involved. It works alongside the ISPS Code — the Code prevents incidents, SUA ensures perpetrators can be prosecuted.

episodes.title: SUA and the ISPS Code Link

title: FAL Convention — Facilitation of Maritime Traffic
description: The Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic (FAL 1965) aims to reduce paperwork and bureaucratic delays for ships entering and leaving ports by standardizing the forms and procedures required by customs, immigration, health, and port authorities worldwide. The nine standard FAL forms define what information ships must submit on arrival. The 2023 amendments mandate a Maritime Single Window system in all member states, moving port formalities to fully electronic submission and transforming how ship agents and masters interact with port authorities.

title: STCW-F 1995 — Standards for Fishing Vessel Personnel
description: The International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Fishing Vessel Personnel (STCW-F 1995) provides the certification framework for officers and crew on fishing vessels of 24 metres and over. Separate from the main STCW Convention, it addresses the specific risks and operational patterns of commercial fishing — including watchkeeping while actively fishing, stability risks from catch handling, and the realities of implementation in national fishing fleets with historically low regulatory compliance.

title: ILO C188 — Work in Fishing Convention
description: The ILO Work in Fishing Convention (C188, 2007, in force 2017) is the MLC 2006 equivalent for the fishing sector, establishing minimum standards for employment agreements, wages, hours of work and rest, accommodation, food, and medical care on fishing vessels over 24 metres. Compliance challenges are significant: fishing operations create irregular work patterns that strain rest hour limits, vessels are often old, and enforcement capacity in fishing flag states varies widely. Understanding C188 is essential for any officer working on regulated fishing vessels.

title: Torremolinos Protocol — Fishing Vessel Safety
description: The Torremolinos International Convention for the Safety of Fishing Vessels (1977) and its 1993 Protocol establish construction, stability, machinery, life-saving, and fire safety standards for fishing vessels of 24 metres and over on international voyages. Fishing vessels were historically excluded from SOLAS, and Torremolinos/its Protocol fills that gap. Compliance and Port State Control application to fishing vessels remain challenging due to the age profile of many national fishing fleets and the diversity of flag state implementation.

title: ISPS Code
description: The International Ship and Port Facility Security Code was fast-tracked by IMO after the 9/11 attacks and entered into force in 2004 as an amendment to SOLAS Chapter XI-2. It establishes a framework of measures to enhance the security of ships and port facilities. The code defines responsibilities for Company Security Officers, Ship Security Officers, and Port Facility Security Officers. It introduces three MARSEC levels that escalate operational security measures in response to changing threat environments.

episodes.title: Why the ISPS Code Was Created

title: IMDG Code
description: The International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code is the global rulebook for transporting dangerous goods in packaged form by sea, implementing SOLAS Chapter VII Part A. It classifies substances into nine hazard classes and assigns UN numbers, Proper Shipping Names, packing groups, stowage codes, and segregation requirements. The code is published biennially and the current edition must always be used on board. It covers the entire chain from classification and packaging through documentation, stowage, segregation, and emergency response.

episodes.title: UN Numbers and the Dangerous Goods List

title: IMSBC Code
description: The International Maritime Solid Bulk Cargoes Code has been mandatory since 2011 and governs all solid cargo transported in bulk, including coal, grain, ore, and nickel ore. It classifies cargoes into three groups: Group A (liquefaction risk), Group B (chemical hazard), and Group C (neither). The code places specific obligations on shippers to provide accurate declarations of cargo properties before loading. Failure to comply has been a contributing factor in multiple bulk carrier losses.

title: IGF Code
description: The International Code of Safety for Ships Using Gases or Other Low-Flashpoint Fuels became mandatory in 2017 as part of SOLAS Chapter II-1 Part G. It applies to ships using LNG, methanol, or other alternative fuels with a flashpoint below 60°C. The code uses a goal-based approach combining prescriptive requirements with equivalency provisions. Specific STCW certification under the Manila Amendments is required for crew serving on ships subject to the code.

title: IGC Code
description: The International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Liquefied Gases in Bulk governs the design and operation of LNG and LPG carriers. It specifies four cargo containment system types and establishes stringent requirements for the primary and secondary barriers protecting the hull from cryogenic cargo. Cargo operations involve unique hazards including cryogenic temperatures, pressurized gas, and the risk of rollover in LNG tanks. STCW Advanced Training for Liquefied Gas Tankers is required for officers serving on these vessels.

title: IBC Code
description: The International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk classifies chemical tankers into three types based on the hazard of cargoes they are permitted to carry. Type I ships may carry the most hazardous chemicals, Type II moderately hazardous, and Type III the least hazardous. The Chapter 17 cargo list in the code specifies the ship type, tank type, and special requirements for each chemical. Tank coating compatibility and cargo sequencing are critical operational concerns on chemical tankers.

title: Polar Code
description: The International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters became mandatory for new ships in 2017 and for existing ships in 2018, supplementing both SOLAS and MARPOL with requirements specific to Arctic and Antarctic waters. Ships are classified into three categories (A, B, C) based on ice capability, and each must carry a Polar Water Operational Manual and a Polar Ship Certificate. The code addresses ice navigation, cold weather operations, emergency response, and strengthened environmental discharge restrictions. STCW training requirements were introduced alongside the code under regulation A-V/4.

seasons.title: Season 3 — Environmental Protection in Polar Waters

episodes.title: MARPOL Annex I — Arctic HFO Ban

title: LSA Code
description: The Life-Saving Appliances Code is the technical standard behind SOLAS Chapter III, specifying performance requirements, test standards, and markings for every type of life-saving appliance on board a ship. A piece of equipment described as "SOLAS-approved" means it has been tested and certified to LSA Code standards. The code covers personal appliances (lifejackets, immersion suits, lifebuoys), pyrotechnics and electronic distress equipment, inflatable and rigid life rafts, totally enclosed lifeboats, and rescue boats.

title: FSS Code
description: The Fire Safety Systems Code is the technical companion to SOLAS Chapter II-2, specifying how fire detection, alarm, suppression, and protection systems must be designed, installed, tested, and maintained. It became mandatory in 2002 and covers everything from smoke detectors and fire alarm panels to CO2 total flooding systems, portable extinguishers, and firemen's outfits. Understanding the FSS Code is essential for any officer responsible for fire safety equipment maintenance.

episodes.title: International Shore Connection and Emergency Fire Pump

title: CSS Code
description: The Code of Safe Practice for Cargo Stowage and Securing provides the methodology for safely stowing and securing non-bulk, non-tanker cargo including containers, vehicles, heavy lifts, and timber. While technically non-mandatory guidelines, SOLAS Regulation VI/5 makes the CSS Code the accepted method for securing force calculations, giving it effective mandatory status. Every ship carrying cargo must have an approved Cargo Securing Manual based on the CSS Code principles.

title: NOx Technical Code
description: The NOx Technical Code (NTC 2008) is the technical specification for testing, certifying, and verifying the NOx emissions of marine diesel engines under MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 13. It establishes three emission tiers with progressively stricter limits and prescribes the test cycles used to certify each engine type. Every diesel engine above 130 kW must hold an Engine International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate, and modifications to certified engines must be managed through a defined approval process.

title: MODU Code
description: The Code for the Construction and Equipment of Mobile Offshore Drilling Units covers semi-submersibles, jackup rigs, and self-propelled drilling ships, supplementing SOLAS with requirements specific to these specialized structures. The 1989 MODU Code (and its 2009 update) addresses stability, structural integrity, fire and gas safety, life-saving appliances, and dynamic positioning. The catastrophic loss of the semi-submersible Alexander Kielland in 1980 was a driving event in the development of purpose-specific stability criteria for MODUs.

seasons.title: Season 2 — Safety Systems on Offshore Units

episodes.title: Fire and Gas Detection on Drilling Units

title: OSV Guidelines
description: The IMO Interim Guidelines for Offshore Supply Vessels and related circulars address the gap between standard SOLAS cargo ship rules and the specialized operational profile of platform supply vessels, anchor handling tug supply vessels, and emergency response and rescue vessels. OSVs carry open deck cargo including liquid mud, drill pipe, and containers to and from offshore installations, creating stability and safety challenges not addressed by standard cargo ship regulations. Crew require both STCW certification and OPITO offshore survival training.

title: Large Yacht Code LY3
description: The MCA Large Yacht Code (LY3) is the UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency's safety standard for commercial yachts over 24 meters operated with guests for hire or reward. It is one of the most widely used superyacht codes internationally, applied by many flag states beyond the UK. LY3 adapts SOLAS-equivalent requirements to the yacht environment and defines certification standards for officers and crew. The combination of professional crew and non-seafaring guests creates specific safety briefing and emergency management challenges.

title: FAO/ILO/IMO Fishing Code
description: The Code of Safety for Fishermen and Fishing Vessels is a joint publication by the Food and Agriculture Organization, the International Labour Organization, and IMO, providing comprehensive safety guidance for the fishing industry. Part A covers fishermen's safety, training, and welfare, while Part B addresses fishing vessel design and stability. Although not itself a mandatory convention, the code is widely referenced in STCW-F certification requirements and national legislation. Fishing is statistically one of the most dangerous occupations in the world, and the code addresses both the occupational hazards of deck work and the fundamental stability challenges unique to fishing vessels.

episodes.title: What is the FAO/ILO/IMO Fishing Code

title: SOLAS Chapter II-1 — Construction, Subdivision & Stability
description: SOLAS Chapter II-1 governs the structural design, subdivision, and stability of ships. It establishes how ships must be divided into watertight compartments and defines the damage stability criteria they must meet. The chapter has been significantly strengthened by the 2009 SOLAS amendments, introducing probabilistic damage stability for all passenger and cargo ships. It also covers machinery and electrical installation requirements, including emergency power and steering gear.

title: SOLAS Chapter II-2 — Fire Protection, Detection & Extinction
description: SOLAS Chapter II-2 is the comprehensive fire safety chapter, applying to all ships and setting out the structural, active, and procedural measures required to prevent, detect, and control shipboard fires. It defines fire zone boundaries, structural fire protection ratings (A, B, and C class divisions), and the fixed suppression systems required in different spaces. The chapter also mandates fire detection systems, personal firefighting equipment, and prescribes drill frequencies and PSC compliance evidence.

title: SOLAS Chapter III — Life-Saving Appliances
description: SOLAS Chapter III sets the carriage, maintenance, and operational requirements for all life-saving appliances on board ships. It distinguishes between cargo ship and passenger ship complement requirements and is backed technically by the LSA Code. The chapter covers lifeboats, liferafts, EPIRBs, SARTs, immersion suits, and Thermal Protective Aids, as well as the drill and inspection schedule required to keep all equipment ready for immediate use.

episodes.title: Immersion Suits and Thermal Protective Aids

title: SOLAS Chapter IV — Radio Communications (GMDSS)
description: SOLAS Chapter IV implements the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS), replacing the old Morse code watchkeeping system with a zone-based satellite and terrestrial communications framework. Equipment requirements scale with the sea area in which the ship operates, from A1 (coastal VHF range) to A4 (polar regions not covered by satellite). The chapter also governs GMDSS maintenance methods and the certification of radio operators.

title: SOLAS Chapter V — Safety of Navigation
description: SOLAS Chapter V is unique in applying to all ships on all voyages, regardless of size or flag. It mandates specific bridge equipment — radar, AIS, ECDIS, VDR — and requires every ship to carry out proper voyage planning. Chapter V also governs hydrographic services, chart accuracy obligations, and the restricted list of legally recognized distress signals.

title: SOLAS Chapter VI — Carriage of Cargoes
description: SOLAS Chapter VI sets the framework for the safe loading, stowage, securing, and documentation of solid bulk cargoes, grain, timber deck cargoes, and fuel oil carried in bulk. It works alongside the IMSBC Code and the International Grain Code as enabling instruments, and places specific obligations on both shippers and masters. The chapter underscores the master's right to refuse cargo when accurate information is not provided.

title: MARPOL Annex I — Oil Pollution Prevention
description: MARPOL Annex I is the foundational oil pollution convention, applying to all ships and placing additional obligations on oil tankers. It governs the overboard discharge of oily bilge water, the maintenance of Oil Record Books, and the structural and operational requirements for tankers. The Annex is enforced through the IOPP Certificate, the OWS inspection regime, and criminal prosecution for deliberate ORB falsification.

seasons.title: Season 1 — Oil Record Book & Discharge Rules

episodes.title: Segregated Ballast Tanks and Double Hull

title: MARPOL Annex II — Noxious Liquid Substances
description: MARPOL Annex II controls the discharge of noxious liquid substances carried in bulk on chemical tankers. Substances are classified into four categories — X, Y, Z, and OS — with Category X posing the greatest environmental hazard and prohibiting any sea discharge. Compliance is evidenced through the NLS Cargo Record Book and the Certificate of Fitness issued under the IBC Code.

title: MARPOL Annex V — Garbage from Ships
description: The 2013 revised MARPOL Annex V fundamentally changed the garbage discharge framework by making total prohibition the default. Only a narrow set of materials — food waste under specific conditions, certain cargo residues, and water from washing biodegradable agents — may still be discharged at sea. The Garbage Management Plan and Garbage Record Book are the primary compliance tools.

episodes.title: Garbage Management Plan and Garbage Record Book

title: MARPOL Annex VI — Air Pollution Prevention
description: MARPOL Annex VI controls air pollution from ships, covering sulphur oxides (SOx), nitrogen oxides (NOx), ozone-depleting substances, and shipboard incineration. The 2020 global sulphur cap was the most significant recent change, dropping the global limit to 0.50% S (m/m). The 2023 EEXI and ongoing CII requirements have extended Annex VI into energy efficiency regulation for both new and existing ships.

episodes.title: Annex VI Scope and IAPP Certificate
Bunker Delivery Notes and Fuel Sampling

title: STCW Regulation II — Deck Officers
description: STCW Chapter II establishes the certification and competency standards for all deck officers, from the Officer of the Watch at operational level through to the Chief Mate and Master at management level. It defines the minimum sea service, the approved training pathways, and the revalidation requirements that keep deck officer certificates in force. PSC enforces these standards directly by verifying seafarer certificates and testing crew knowledge during inspections.

episodes.title: The Certificate of Competency for OOW
Regulation II/2 — Chief Mate and Master

title: STCW Regulation III — Engine Officers
description: STCW Chapter III defines the certification and competency requirements for engine department officers, from the Officer in Charge of an Engineering Watch at operational level through to the Chief Engineer and Second Engineer at management level. It also covers the Electro-Technical Officer certification introduced by the Manila 2010 amendments and the Engine Room Resource Management training now required at management level.

seasons.title: Season 2 — Chief Engineer and Management Level

episodes.title: Regulation III/2 — Chief Engineer and Second Engineer

title: STCW Regulation V — Special Training Requirements
description: STCW Chapter V imposes additional training and endorsement requirements on seafarers serving on specialized vessels — tankers, passenger ships (including ro-ro ferries), and vessels with dynamic positioning systems. These endorsements sit on top of the standard CoC and must be renewed separately. The chapter was substantially expanded by the Manila 2010 amendments to add DP operator certification.

episodes.title: Regulation V/1-2 — Liquefied Gas Tanker Training

title: STCW Regulation V/3 — Fishing Vessel Officers
description: STCW Regulation V/3 addresses the training and certification of officers on fishing vessels, linking the mainstream STCW Convention to the dedicated STCW-F 1995 Convention. It sets out the skipper, mate, and chief engineer certification pathways for fishing vessels and acknowledges that the unique hazards of fishing operations require adapted safety training content.

title: STCW-F — Specific Regulations
description: The STCW-F 1995 Convention is the dedicated international instrument for the training and certification of fishing vessel personnel. It mirrors the structure of STCW but adapts every element — certification, watchkeeping, and training standards — to the specific operational environment of commercial fishing. Implementation remains uneven globally, with significant variations between flag states and regional fishing areas.

title: Panama Flag State Regulations
description: Panama operates the world's largest open ship registry by tonnage and its regulatory framework — administered by the Autoridad Maritima de Panama (AMP) — shapes the working lives of hundreds of thousands of seafarers. This series covers AMP certification processes, Panama seafarer documents, the Panama Canal Authority's vessel requirements, and the interaction between Panamanian law, MLC 2006, and international PSC enforcement.

episodes.title: Port State Control and the Panama Flag

title: MLC 2006 — Titles 1 to 5 Compliance
description: The Maritime Labour Convention 2006 is the fourth pillar of international shipping law, setting minimum standards for seafarer employment, accommodation, medical care, welfare, and enforcement. Its five Titles are implemented through the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance (DMLC), which requires every shipowner to document how their ships comply with each national regulation that gives effect to the Convention.

episodes.title: MLC Title 4 — Medical Care at Sea

title: MOU and Port State Control
description: Port State Control is the primary enforcement mechanism for international shipping conventions, allowing coastal states to inspect foreign-flagged vessels in their ports. The nine regional Memoranda of Understanding coordinate PSC across the world, share inspection data, and publish targeting criteria that determine which ships face the highest inspection frequency. Understanding how PSC works — from ship selection through to detention and appeal — is essential knowledge for every seafarer and ship manager.

title: Terrestrial Navigation
description: Covers the full scope of traditional ship navigation from chart reading and position fixing to celestial observations and ocean passage planning. Officers learn to calculate tidal windows, apply compass corrections, and construct dead reckoning plots with confidence. Coastal pilotage techniques including parallel indexing and radar navigation are covered in depth. The series concludes with celestial navigation and great circle route planning for offshore passages.

title: ECDIS and Electronic Navigation
description: A comprehensive guide to ECDIS from carriage requirements and chart database management to route planning, monitoring, and failure procedures. Officers learn to configure safety parameters correctly, manage ENC updates, and understand the legal implications of ECDIS-only passage plans. The series also covers AIS integration, cyber security risks in navigation systems, and the IMO e-Navigation strategy shaping the future of the bridge.

title: Radar and ARPA
description: Builds competence in radar operation from basic principles through ARPA target tracking and collision avoidance decision-making. Officers learn the critical difference between true and relative vectors, how to set CPA/TCPA alarms appropriately, and why ARPA is an aid — not a substitute for COLREGS judgment. Practical radar navigation techniques including parallel indexing and restricted visibility procedures are covered in the final season.

episodes.title: Radar and Collision Avoidance Decision Making

title: Marine Meteorology
description: Equips seafarers to read synoptic charts, interpret on-board barometric trends, and make informed decisions about tropical cyclone avoidance and heavy weather routing. The series covers atmospheric fundamentals including Coriolis effect and frontal systems, then progresses to practical at-sea observation skills and use of GRIB data and weather services. Dangerous phenomena such as sea fog, waterspouts, and rogue waves are addressed with clear recognition and avoidance guidance.

title: Ship Stability
description: Provides a thorough grounding in stability theory and its practical application across loading, trimming, damage scenarios, and heavy weather. Officers learn to interpret GZ curves, apply the IS Code criteria, calculate free surface effect, and use the loading manual and stability computer correctly. The series closes with damage stability principles, heavy weather rolling phenomena, and stability considerations unique to RoRo, passenger, offshore, and fishing vessel types.

seasons.title: Season 3 — Damage Stability and Special Cases

title: Cargo Handling Operations
description: Covers the full scope of cargo operations from passage planning and stowage to container management, bulk loading sequences, and dangerous goods integration. Officers learn how to prepare and execute a cargo plan that balances weight distribution, stability, access, and segregation requirements. The series also addresses the legal aspects of cargo damage and claims, including the correct use of the ship's log, mate's receipts, and noting protests.

seasons.title: Season 2 — Special Cargo and Safe Practice

title: Dangerous Goods at Sea
description: Provides the knowledge to safely accept, stow, segregate, and respond to incidents involving IMDG-classified dangerous goods. Officers learn to navigate the Dangerous Goods List, verify documentation, apply stowage and segregation codes, and use the EmS and MFAG guides under pressure. Reporting obligations under MARPOL Annex III and SOLAS are covered alongside the practical realities of DG handling at the berth.

title: Fire Fighting at Sea
description: Builds competence in fire prevention, equipment use, and coordinated shipboard fire response across all vessel types. From hotwork permits and engine room housekeeping to SCBA donning, CO2 system activation, and boundary cooling tactics, every essential skill is covered. The series concludes with shipboard fire organization, engine room emergency procedures, and the post-fire investigation and reporting obligations under the ISM Code.

episodes.title: Fire Risk Areas on Different Ships
Boundary Cooling and Fire Hose Operations

title: Survival at Sea
description: Covers the complete abandon-ship sequence from the first alarm signal through lifeboat and liferaft boarding to surviving in the raft until rescue. Officers and ratings learn HELP position, boarding procedures, immediate priorities after embarkation, and the physiology of hypothermia and dehydration. Signaling for rescue — from EPIRB activation to parachute flares and SART — is covered in practical detail.

title: Medical First Aid at Sea
description: Prepares officers to manage medical emergencies at sea in the absence of a ship's doctor, covering the STCW Advanced Medical First Aid certification requirements, the ship's medical chest, and telemedicine coordination with TMAS. The series addresses primary survey, CPR/AED, trauma management, and major medical emergencies including stroke and ACS, culminating in medevac decision-making and MRCC coordination procedures.

episodes.title: Medical First Aid vs. Elementary First Aid

title: ERM — Engine Room Resource Management
description: The engineering equivalent of BRM: developing the team communication, situational awareness, and decision-making skills required for safe engine room management. Officers examine how authority gradients and alarm fatigue contribute to machinery casualties, and practice structured communication during handovers, emergencies, and drills. Post-incident debrief technique and ISM non-conformity reporting as a learning mechanism are addressed throughout.

episodes.title: What is ERM and Why It Exists
Situational Awareness in the Engine Room
Emergency Decision Making in the Engine Room

title: GMDSS Operations
description: Covers the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System from its four sea areas and equipment architecture through VHF/MF/HF DSC operation, Inmarsat terminals, NAVTEX, and SAR communication coordination. Officers learn to send a MAYDAY DSC alert, receive and interpret NAVTEX bulletins, and maintain the GMDSS Radio Log. The practical and legal requirements for GMDSS maintenance and annual testing are addressed alongside the GOC/ROC certification pathway.

title: Leadership and Team Management
description: Develops the leadership and teamworking competencies required at STCW management level, with a focus on the unique challenges of multinational maritime crews operating in high-stakes, remote environments. The series examines leadership styles, authority and accountability under maritime law, cross-cultural communication barriers, and the fatigue management obligations that fall on every officer in a position of authority.

title: Environmental Stewardship at Sea
description: Builds awareness and operational competence in environmental protection across pollution prevention, energy efficiency, and incident response. The series covers MARPOL obligations in daily practice, CII and SEEMP requirements for OOW energy awareness, SOPEP activation, and the Ballast Water Management Convention. Voluntary best-practice measures beyond regulatory minimums are highlighted to connect environmental responsibility with commercial and reputational value.

title: Security Awareness
description: Delivers the STCW VI/6-1 Security Awareness Training required of all seafarers under the Manila 2010 amendments, covering threat recognition, high-risk area procedures, SSAS operation, access control, and security incident reporting. The series distinguishes clearly between baseline Awareness Training and the fuller SSO certification, and provides practical guidance on applying BMP6 best management practices in piracy-prone waters.

title: Dynamic Positioning Operations
description: Provides an introduction to DP systems, positioning reference redundancy, failure modes, and the Nautical Institute certification pathway for officers working aboard DP-classed vessels. The series covers DP Class 1, 2, and 3 distinctions, FMEA requirements, operational procedures during offshore tasks including SIMOPS, and the IMCA incident reporting scheme that drives fleet-wide learning.

episodes.title: DP Sensors and Positioning Reference Systems

title: Anchor Handling Operations
description: Covers AHTS vessel operations for running and retrieving anchors for MODUs and semi-submersibles, with a strong emphasis on the deck safety hazards that make anchor handling one of the most dangerous offshore activities. Officers learn the sequence for anchor running and retrieval, the function of deck machinery including shark jaws and the stern roller, and the critical snap-back and kill-zone hazards that have caused fatalities in this sector.

title: HUET and Helicopter Survival
description: Prepares offshore seafarers for helicopter operations and underwater escape from a ditched helicopter, covering pre-flight safety briefings, the HUET pool certification exercise, and post-ditching survival priorities. The series addresses helideck safety, EBS use, capsize and exit technique, hypothermia in cold-water environments, and the SAR response timeline that determines survival outcomes.

title: Fishing Gear Operations
description: Covers the types of commercial fishing gear, their deployment and retrieval sequences, and the deck machinery safety hazards that make fishing one of the most dangerous occupations at sea. Officers and ratings learn snag and entanglement risks during hauling, the emergency stop procedures for net drums and winches, and the specific MOB dangers created by moving gear — including cold water drowning statistics for the fishing sector.

title: Catch Handling and Fish Safety
description: Addresses the stability risks of large catches on deck, the confined space atmosphere hazards in fish holds, and the cold chain and food safety requirements that govern catch quality from sea to market. Officers learn the H2S and CO2 dangers associated with fish holds, the RSW system and its maintenance, and how rapid catch processing connects directly to vessel safety through weight and free surface management.

title: Yacht Seamanship
description: Covers seamanship, weather routing, and regulatory compliance specific to commercial yachts and superyachts, including sailing yacht handling, anchoring techniques, and MCA LY3 manning requirements. Officers learn how to manage non-seafarer guests safely, apply the Commercial Endorsement rules, and navigate the intersection of charter commercial pressure and ISPS safety obligations for large yachts on international voyages.

title: Passenger Safety Management
description: Covers the STCW crowd management and crisis management training requirements for passenger ship and commercial yacht crew, including mustering non-crew passengers, directing evacuation flows, and accommodating persons with reduced mobility. The series addresses the additional MOB complexity on passenger vessels, crisis management decision-making at Master and HoD level, and the post-incident passenger welfare obligations.

episodes.title: Man Overboard on a Passenger Ship

title: Tanker Operations
description: Provides a structured introduction to tanker cargo systems, inert gas management, and the procedures for loading and discharging petroleum cargoes safely. Officers learn the IGS sequence and alarm thresholds, tank entry enclosed space requirements, crude oil washing, and the pressure surge risks at emergency shutdown. The series concludes with OCIMF SIRE 2.0 vetting inspection expectations and what a poor SIRE result means commercially.

episodes.title: Entry into Enclosed Spaces on Tankers

title: Gas Carrier Operations
description: Covers LNG and LPG cargo systems, containment types, inerting and cool-down sequences, and the management of boil-off gas, with particular attention to the cryogenic, rollover, and rapid phase transition hazards unique to gas carrier operations. Officers learn the emergency shutdown system, cargo leak response sequence, and the full STCW certification path from Basic to Advanced Training for Liquefied Gas Tankers required on their Certificate of Competency.

title: ISGOTT — International Safety Guide for Oil Tankers and Terminals
description: ISGOTT (6th edition) is the definitive safety manual for crude and product tanker operations and their interface with shore terminals. Published jointly by ICS, OCIMF, and IAPH, it is not an IMO convention but is so widely adopted that it is treated as mandatory by major charterers and terminal operators. Understanding ISGOTT is essential for any officer involved in tanker cargo operations, and it is central to SIRE 2.0 vetting inspections.

episodes.title: What is ISGOTT and How It Is Used

seasons.title: Season 3 — Gas Hazards and Hot Work

title: OCIMF SIRE 2.0 — Ship Inspection Report Programme
description: SIRE 2.0 (launched 2022) is the major overhaul of OCIMF's Ship Inspection Report Programme — the most important vetting standard for tankers. Replacing SIRE 1.0, the new version uses observation-based assessments instead of yes/no checklists, integrating human factors, safety culture evaluation, and digital reporting. A SIRE 2.0 result can determine whether a tanker gets chartered or sits idle — understanding it is commercially critical for any officer on a tanker.

title: OCIMF MEG4 — Mooring Equipment Guidelines
description: MEG4 (Mooring Equipment Guidelines, 4th edition, 2018) is OCIMF's comprehensive standard for mooring equipment design, selection, inspection, and operation. It replaced MEG3 to address the rising fatality rate from mooring failures and snapback incidents. MEG4 is referenced in SIRE, CDI, and RightShip vetting inspections, and many flag states and terminal operators require MEG4-compliant mooring equipment and procedures.

title: OCIMF OSV Recommendations
description: OCIMF's recommendations for Offshore Support Vessels cover design and construction guidelines, manning, and operational procedures for Platform Supply Vessels (PSV), Anchor Handling Tug Supply vessels (AHTS), and Emergency Response and Rescue Vessels (ERRV). While not binding in the way of IMO conventions, these guidelines are referenced in OVID vetting and by major oil company operators. Understanding OCIMF OSV standards is essential for officers working in the offshore support sector.

title: OCIMF TMSA — Tanker Management and Self Assessment
description: TMSA (Tanker Management and Self Assessment) is OCIMF's framework for assessing a shipping company's safety management system. Companies submit annual self-assessments against 12 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), each with 4 stages of performance. TMSA scores are submitted to OCIMF and shared with charterers who use them as part of their approval process. Understanding TMSA is essential for shore-based managers and senior officers who want to understand the commercial safety expectations of the oil major charterers.

title: CDI — Chemical Tanker Inspection Scheme
description: The CDI (Chemical Distribution Institute) Marine inspection scheme is the chemical tanker equivalent of OCIMF SIRE. CDI inspections verify a chemical tanker's compliance with the IBC Code, MARPOL Annex II, and cargo operator requirements. CDI reports are stored in a database accessible to cargo owners and charterers, and a poor CDI result can prevent a chemical tanker from loading for major shippers. CDI is distinct from SIRE and covers aspects of chemical tanker operations not addressed in the oil tanker vetting framework.

title: OPITO BOSIET — Basic Offshore Safety Induction and Emergency Training
description: BOSIET (Basic Offshore Safety Induction and Emergency Training) is the mandatory safety certification for everyone who works offshore, whether on platforms, FPSOs, or offshore support vessels. Issued under the OPITO (Offshore Petroleum Industry Training Organization) standard, it covers sea survival, firefighting, first aid, and helicopter underwater escape training (HUET). BOSIET is typically required before a first offshore trip and must be renewed every 4 years (FOET refresher).

episodes.title: What is BOSIET and Who Needs It

title: OPITO HUET — Helicopter Underwater Escape Training
description: OPITO HUET (Helicopter Underwater Escape Training) is the standalone version of the underwater escape component of BOSIET for workers who already hold the full BOSIET certificate and need to maintain the helicopter escape skill. HUET trains participants to exit a simulated helicopter cabin after it inverts and sinks — the scenario in an offshore helicopter ditching. The training is physically demanding and must be renewed as part of the FOET cycle. Understanding HUET requirements and procedures is essential for any seafarer working in an offshore helicopter-served environment.

title: DP Operator Certificate (Nautical Institute)
description: The Nautical Institute DP Operator Certificate is the global standard for certification of Dynamic Positioning officers. While not an IMO convention requirement (STCW V/3 references it), the NI DP Certificate is required by virtually all major offshore operators and is specified in every DP vessel charter party. The certificate has two levels: DP Limited (for vessels in limited operations with DP1/2) and DP Unlimited (for all DP operations including deepwater DP3). Understanding the NI DP certificate path is essential for any officer planning an offshore career.

title: ICS Bridge Procedures Guide
description: The ICS Bridge Procedures Guide (6th edition) is the most widely used practical reference for shipboard navigation procedures and bridge team management. Published by the International Chamber of Shipping, it is not a mandatory regulation but is used as the industry standard for developing company-specific bridge procedures manuals. Port State Control inspectors, vetting inspectors, and accident investigators routinely reference the ICS Bridge Procedures Guide when evaluating a ship's navigational safety culture.

title: ICS Tanker Safety Guide
description: The ICS Tanker Safety Guide (Liquefied Gas, Chemicals, or Oil — separate volumes) provides comprehensive guidance for safe tanker operations, complementing ISGOTT and the MARPOL/IBC/IGC regulatory framework. Published by ICS in conjunction with OCIMF, these guides cover everything from pre-arrival planning to emergency procedures specific to tanker cargo types. They are referenced in SIRE and CDI vetting and form the basis for many company SMS procedures on tanker fleets.

episodes.title: Using ICS Guides in SMS Development

title: RightShip GHG Rating
description: RightShip is an independent maritime risk assessment company whose vetting services are used extensively by dry bulk charterers (BHP, Rio Tinto, etc.) and some container operators. The RightShip GHG Rating (A-G scale) assesses a vessel's carbon efficiency relative to comparable ships and is increasingly used in chartering decisions alongside the IMO CII rating. Ships with a poor RightShip GHG rating or low safety score face reduced chartering opportunities in the dry bulk and bulk liquid sectors.

title: IMCA DP Standards
description: IMCA (International Marine Contractors Association) is the body that sets industry standards for offshore marine operations, particularly DP. IMCA documents (M 103, M 117, M 190, D 007) govern DP vessel capability assessments, incident reporting, operations guidance, and competence standards. Compliance with IMCA DP standards is required by oil majors, offshore operators, and insurers. IMCA M 117 (DP incident reporting) is the most widely cited document in the offshore industry's safety learning system.

title: OCIMF OVID — Offshore Vessel Inspection Database
description: OCIMF OVID (Offshore Vessel Inspection Database) is the offshore equivalent of the SIRE tanker vetting database. OVID stores inspection reports for offshore support vessels — PSVs, AHTSs, ERRVs — conducted against the OCIMF/IMCA Offshore Vessel Inspection Questionnaire (OVIQ). Oil company operators use OVID results when approving offshore support vessels for charter. An OVID inspection covers vessel condition, safety systems, DP capability, crew competence, and compliance with OCIMF OSV recommendations and IMCA standards.

episodes.title: OVID and SIRE on the Same Vessel
